full_judgment:
13. The learned Counsel Mr Syed Mokaddas Ali with Mr Biswajit Chakraborty, appearing on behalf of the defendant-respondent-petitioner, submits that the learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria was absolutely wrong and erroneous in reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court. The learned trial Court, after examining the evidence on record and discussing all the issues framed by him whether the suit is maintainable in its present form or not and other issues, passed the judgment and decree dismissing the suit of the plaintiff which was hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. Next he submits that the learned trial Court committed no error in. deciding the issues and rightly held that the plaintiff miserably failed to prove the case, as such, the judgment and decree passed by the learned trial Court was absolutely right and justified which should not be assailed by the learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria. Mr Syed Mokaddas Ali next submits that the lower appellate Court while reversing the finding of the trial Court he should assign a cogent and reasonable ground and the finding of the trial Court should be reversed with reference to the evidence on record, but the learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria committed a gross illegality in not referring the finding of the trial Court, particularly with regard to the law point which is liable to be set aside and interfered by this Court. Mr Syed Mokaddas Ali further submits that the finding of the trial Court, particularly on 2 points, that the suit is hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and the plaintiff No. 2 during the pendency of the trial of the suit by submitting a compromise petition and relinquished his claim over 20 decimals of the suit land in Plot Nos. 166-167 and accordingly, the plaintiff Nos. 1-3 ought to have corrected the schedule of the suit land. But the lower appellate Court did not mention a single word in his judgment on these two points i.e. with regard to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and the compromise petition filed by the plaintiff No. 2 who has relinquished his claim and also did not file any appeal. This sort of non-consideration in finding of the lower appellate Court in reversing the judgment of the trial Court appears to be manifestly perverse which is liable to be interfered by this Court. The learned Counsel finally submits that admittedly the defendants had been in possession of the suit land since long so in a suit for declaration without seeking a consequential relief for recovery of khas possession is not at all maintainable. The PWs 2 and 3 in cross-examination categorically stated in their evidence that Deen Mohammed, the defendant No. 2, had been living in the suit land with his family members by erecting houses. PW 3 further stated in his evidence that defendant No. 2 Deen Mohammad was a good man and he was in possession of the suit land. He also submits that the lower appellate Court did not at all discuss the evidence of PWs and DWs. Md Ruhul Amin, son of Deen Mohammad was examined as DW 1 and after the death of Deen Mohammad during the pendency of the suit who was living in the suit land categorically stated in his evidence about the title and possession of the suit land and exhibited the registered title deed in original dated 25-11-68 which was exhibited as Exhibit-Ka. The registered deed Exhibit-Ka, the original purchase deed of the defendant obviously shows that the vendor of that deed Kulsum and Tara Banu along with others were the vendor who are now plaintiff Nos. 1-3 respectively and in that deed the vendee was Deen Mohammad the defendant No. 2 and since the purchase of the suit land in the year 1968 after the death of Badsha Mia the defendant has been living in the suit land with his other family members. 

 15. On a meticulous examination of the evidence on record, exhibits, registered deed, documents and also the judgment of both the Courts below it appears that the trial Court discussed the evidence and also perused the documents and legal aspect of the case and made his observation that the suit was hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The learned trial Court further held in his judgment that since PWs 2 and 3 admitted the possession of the defendant in the suit land the plaintiff ought to have sought for recovery of khas possession as consequential relief. But the plaintiff instituted a simple suit for declaration of title which is not maintainable and hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria while reversing the judgment of the trial Court did not write a single word about this specific finding of the law point by the trial Court which appears to be manifestly perverse. Moreover, when the plaintiff No. 2 during the pendency of the suit in the trial Court by submitting a compromise petition relinquished his claim over 20 decimals of the suit land then the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 3 ought to have amended the schedule of the suit land but the plaintiffs did not do so. This observation made by the trial Court was absolutely correct but the lower appellate Court did not at all consider this vital and material point and did not mention anything in his judgment on this point. The lower appellate Court while reversing the judgment of the trial Court is required to reverse the material finding of the trial Court with reference to the evidence on record but the learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria did not do so. The lower appellate Court should assign cogent and reasonable ground in reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court.
